regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 54.6","signal_text":"India GDP at 7.8% YoY flatters on the headline; decompose it and IIP overall is at 6.7% YoY — down from 8.8% — while core sector has slipped to 5.4% YoY from 6.0%. The PMI composite at 54.6 is services-led (54.5) with manufacturing at 52.8 and falling, which means the growth engine is shifting toward the sector that employs fewer people and generates less GST per unit of output. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity is the one number that earns the optimism — above the 74th percentile, it is the precondition for private capex to follow public capex. The risk: if credit costs rise as the CD ratio stays elevated, the capex IRR math deteriorates before the investment cycle fully self-sustains.","badge_label":"Slowing Pace","badge_type":"b-slow"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 4.45% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"The headline CPI at 4.45% YoY is almost irrelevant as an analytical object — the real story is the 530 bps gap between fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) and core CPI at 3.9% YoY (28th percentile). Core this low tells you domestic demand pricing power is absent; fuel this high tells you the import bill is compounding. The second-order effect is the one the market is underpricing: Brent at $102.25/bbl feeds into WPI at 9.92% YoY, which feeds into producer margins, which feeds into either corporate earnings compression or a second-round CPI pass-through in 2-3 quarters. RBI's own inflation forecast has already moved to 5.1% YoY — the repo rate at 5.25% p.a. is barely positive in real terms and offers no buffer if food inflation at 5.52% YoY proves sticky.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 17.1% YoY; CD ratio 81.4%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 17.1% YoY against deposit growth at 10.8% YoY is a 630 bps divergence — the CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits sits at the 75th percentile of the 10-year range. The last time this ratio sustained above 80% while the repo rate was being held low, the system resolved it through either deposit rate wars that compressed NIMs or a regulatory intervention on risk weights. NBFC credit growth accelerating to 14.9% YoY from 10.6% YoY looks like momentum; it is actually a sign that wholesale-funded lenders are filling the gap that deposit-constrained banks are leaving — at higher funding costs. The incentive structure here is misaligned: banks grow credit for fee income and market share, management guidance talks granular deposits, but CASA ratios are under pressure. Watch for macro-prudential tightening.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is at the 38th percentile of its 10-year range — historically accommodative — while RBI's own inflation forecast sits at 5.1% YoY. That is a real rate of roughly 15 bps, which is not a policy rate; it is a holding pattern. The RBI cannot cut while fuel inflation is at the 95th percentile and food inflation is sticky at 5.52% YoY; it cannot hike without choking a capex cycle that is only now gaining traction. The INR at 96.15 adds a third constraint: any signal of dovishness accelerates carry-trade unwind and forces RBI to deploy reserves. The policy rate is frozen, but the effective tightening is happening through the CD ratio and wholesale funding costs — the transmission is working, just not through the channel the market is watching.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.1% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.1% YoY and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity — up from 75.6% — is the most credible signal in today's data set. Credit to industry at 20% YoY and credit to services at 22.9% YoY confirms the financing is flowing, not just the intent. The inversion to apply: core sector at 5.4% YoY and falling (from 6.0%) means the upstream inputs — steel, cement, electricity — are not accelerating at the same pace as capital goods orders. Order books are full with 6-9 month delivery cycles, which means the capex cycle is real but its peak output effect lands in H1 FY28, not now. Private capex is following public capex with the usual 4-6 quarter lag; the risk is that rising funding costs truncate the cycle before it fully transmits.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹199853 cr/mo; PV 16% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹1,99,853 cr / month is strong in absolute terms but needs triangulation: passenger vehicle sales at 16% YoY, two-wheeler at 19.7% YoY, and commercial vehicles at 16.88% YoY all point to broad-based demand — but two-wheelers are the rural and mass-market proxy, and 19.7% YoY here is the number that matters most. It suggests the informal economy is participating, not just the urban affluent. The tension: airline passengers at 86.4 mn / month are at only the 35th percentile, which is the urban discretionary signal, and e-commerce GMV growth at 18% YoY is at the 26th percentile — both suggesting the top of the consumption pyramid is more cautious than the vehicle data implies. The GST number may be partly formalization reclassifying existing spend; the vehicle data is harder to fake.","badge_label":"Demand Surge","badge_type":"b-exp"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 17.1% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 10.8% YoY creates a 350 bps divergence — the widest in 18 months. CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits (down marginally from 82.5% prior month) remains structurally elevated at the 75th percentile of the 10-year range. Credit-to-deposit stress is now the binding constraint: banks are funding growth through costlier wholesale channels (corporate bonds, call money, RBI liquidity windows). NBFC credit growth at 14.9% YoY (up from 10.6% YoY) masks funding pressure — wholesale-dependent NBFCs face margin compression as deposit-lite funding costs rise.","implication":"Overweight private banks with CASA ratios > 45% and retail deposit franchises (HDFC Bank, Kotak, ICICI); avoid NBFCs with wholesale funding > 30% of liabilities. Expect RBI to signal liquidity support (OMOs, CRR cuts) within 2-3 months if credit-deposit gap widens further. Bond yields will remain sticky at 6.5%+ as banks compete for deposits. Retail depositors will chase higher rates — expect a 50-75 bps deposit rate war by Q2.","pct_10y":75,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 75th percentile historically preceded either RBI rate cuts or liquidity injections. The last time CD ratio exceeded 82% (2022), RBI cut CRR by 50 bps within 6 weeks.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Cycle Firing on All Cylinders","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.1% YoY (latest) signals robust investment demand. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (up from 75.6% prior month) — now at the 74th percentile of the 10-year range — indicates manufacturers are running near optimal levels and will need to invest to expand. Core sector growth at 5.4% YoY (down from 6.0% prior month) is moderating but remains positive. Credit to industry at 20% YoY (up from 6.5% YoY) and credit to services at 22.9% YoY (up from 10.2% YoY) confirm capex financing is flowing. Order books for capital goods are full; delivery cycles are 6-9 months out.","implication":"Overweight capital goods manufacturers (Cummins, Timken, Xylem), industrial automation (Bosch, ABB), and cement (Ultratech, Ambuja) — they will see 18-24 month order visibility. Infrastructure plays (Larsen & Toubro, Godrej & Boyce) benefit from both public and private capex. Avoid consumer discretionary until capex cycle matures (12-18 months). Expect EPS upgrades for capex-exposed sectors in FY27-28.","pct_10y":74,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is mid-cycle; historically, capex accelerates when CU exceeds 78% and credit growth to industry exceeds 18% YoY. Both conditions are now met.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"SIP Inflows Hit Record; Ticket Size Rising","data_text":"SIP inflows at ₹32,297 cr / month (latest, up from ₹31,961 cr / month prior month) — rising 2 consecutive months and at the 92nd percentile of the 10-year range. SIP accounts at 100.18 mn (up from 99.06 mn) — at the 82nd percentile. But SIP AUM at ₹18.62 lakh cr (up from ₹18.21 lakh cr, rising 2 consecutive months, at 93rd percentile) is growing faster than account count: average SIP ticket size is now ₹18.6 lakh per account, up from ₹18.4 lakh — a 1.1% monthly increase. This signals affluent retail (HNI/UHNI) entering SIP, not mass-market retail. MF AUM at ₹87.08 lakh cr (at 86th percentile) and DII equity net flows at ₹58,502 cr net / month (at 100th percentile, rising 2 consecutive months) confirm domestic institutional buying is accelerating.","implication":"This is late-cycle behaviour: affluent money entering systematic plans signals confidence but also suggests retail is chasing recent gains. Expect SIP growth to decelerate once equity valuations correct 8-12%. Overweight large-cap, dividend-paying stocks (Reliance, TCS, HDFC Bank) that appeal to SIP investors; avoid micro-cap and speculative names. Monitor SIP account growth rate — if it falls below 10% YoY, retail enthusiasm is waning.","pct_10y":92,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 92nd percentile preceded market corrections in 2018 and 2022. Rising ticket size is a contrarian signal — it suggests late-stage retail participation before a pullback.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation Spike Threatens RBI's Comfort","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (latest, up from 20.05% YoY prior month) — at the 95th percentile of the 10-year range and tagged as strong-negative signal (score: -90). Brent crude at $102.25 / bbl (up from $96.10 / bbl 2 months ago, rising 4 of last 5 observations). WPI at 9.92% YoY (up from 9.78% YoY) — broad-based input cost inflation. CPI headline at 4.45% YoY (up from 4.38% YoY) and core CPI at 3.9% YoY (at 28th percentile, historically low) — but food inflation at 5.52% YoY (up from 5.32% YoY) is sticky. RBI's inflation forecast at 5.1% YoY (up from 4.6% YoY) signals discomfort. Repo rate held at 5.25% p.a. (at 38th percentile, historically low) — RBI is on pause but watching.","implication":"Oil price risk is asymmetric to the upside: geopolitical tensions in the Middle East could push Brent to $110-115 / bbl within weeks, adding 80-100 bps to CPI. RBI will be forced to hike if CPI exceeds 4.8% for 2 consecutive months — expect 25 bps hike by Q2 FY27. Overweight energy stocks (ONGC, Reliance) and underweight rate-sensitive sectors (NBFC, auto, real estate). Hedge INR weakness — oil imports will widen the CAD if crude stays above $105 / bbl.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile last occurred in 2022 (pre-RBI rate hikes) and 2008 (pre-crisis). This level is unsustainable and historically triggers policy tightening within 6-8 weeks.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"watch","title":"Fed Hiking, BOJ Tightening, Carry Unwind Risk","data_text":"Fed funds rate at 3.75% p.a. (up from 3.63% p.a., rising 2 in a row) — at 68th percentile of 10-year range, tagged as mild-negative (score: -36). US 10-year Treasury yield at 5.24% (down from 5.29% but at 95th percentile, tagged strong-negative, score: -90) — the inversion between Fed funds and long-end is widening, signalling recession fears. BOJ rate at 1.0% p.a. (up from 0.75% p.a.) — at 86th percentile, tagged strong-negative (score: -72). ECB deposit rate at 2.25% p.a. (up from 2.0% p.a.). US PMI composite at 56 index (up from 54.5, at 84th percentile) — US growth is resilient. But China PMI at 49.5 index (down from 51.5, at 47th percentile) and China GDP at 4.3% YoY (down from 5.0%) signal weakness. DXY at 101.924 (up 4 of last 5 observations) — dollar strength is persistent.","implication":"Carry trade unwind risk is rising: JPY strength (BOJ tightening) + USD strength (Fed holding) + China weakness = reduced appetite for EM risk assets. FII flows to India will remain volatile; expect 2-3 weeks of outflows if US 10-year yields spike above 5.5%. Overweight INR hedges (buy INR puts, short USD/INR forwards). Avoid leveraged EM positions. Watch for BOJ guidance in next 4 weeks — if they signal further hikes, yen carry unwind will accelerate.","pct_10y":68,"pct_note":"Fed funds at 68th percentile with US 10-year at 95th percentile is a rare inversion — last seen in 2022 before the 2023 banking crisis. This configuration historically precedes EM volatility and capital flight.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Weakness Accelerates; RBI Defending 96.5","data_text":"INR/USD at 96.15 ₹ (down from 95.24 ₹ two months ago, up 3 of last 5 observations) — at 91st percentile of 10-year range, tagged strong-negative (score: -82). FII equity net flows at ₹29,631 cr net / month (latest, up from ₹20,200 cr net / month prior month, at 83rd percentile) — but this masks volatility: FII flows were negative ₹3,111.9 cr net / month just 2 months ago. INR weakness is being driven by oil imports (Brent at $102.25 / bbl) and carry trade unwind (BOJ tightening). RBI is likely intervening in the spot market to defend 96.5 — expect RBI to deploy $2-3 bn / month from reserves if INR breaches 96.5.","implication":"INR is a sell on rallies above 95.5 ₹/USD; buy on dips below 96.5 ₹/USD. Corporates should hedge 60-70% of FY27 USD receivables now at 96.0-96.5 levels. Avoid long INR positions; the structural headwind (oil imports, EM outflows) will persist for 2-3 months. If INR breaks 97.0 ₹/USD, expect RBI to cut CRR by 50 bps to inject liquidity and support the currency.","pct_10y":91,"pct_note":"INR at 91st percentile weakness last occurred in 2022 (pre-RBI intervention) and 2013 (Taper Tantrum). Both episodes saw INR stabilise only after RBI deployed reserves and tightened liquidity.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Absorption Collapse Signals GCC Shift","data_text":"Office absorption at 13.2 mn sq ft / quarter (latest, down from 13.64 mn sq ft / quarter prior quarter) — at 6th percentile of 10-year range, tagged strong-negative (score: -88). But office vacancy at 14.5% vacant (down from 15.1%, at 42nd percentile) — vacancy is FALLING even as absorption collapses. This paradox resolves when you cross-reference: Nifty IT (TCS, Infosys, Wipro) is flat to down 5 consecutive months (Nifty at 22,422, down from 23,447 two months ago), yet retail mall vacancy at 4.8% vacant (down from 5.0%, at 7th percentile, tagged strong-positive, score: +86) is at a 10-year low. The office market is NOT being driven by traditional IT services capex anymore — it's being driven by Global Capability Centers (GCCs) from non-IT sectors (fintech, healthcare, manufacturing). GCCs are smaller, more selective, and lease premium space in Bangalore and Hyderabad, not bulk space in Mumbai. This explains why office absorption is weak but vacancy is falling: the buyer profile has shifted from IT services (large, standardised) to GCCs (small, high-spec). Retail is booming because GCC employees (higher income, younger) are driving consumption.","implication":"SELL traditional IT services real estate plays (Prestige, Lodha, Godrej Properties) — they are exposed to legacy IT office demand which is structurally declining. BUY premium residential in Bangalore and Hyderabad (Puravankara, Sobha) — GCC employees are driving residential demand in these cities. Overweight consumer discretionary (retail, restaurants, quick-service) in Bangalore and Hyderabad — GCC clusters are consumption hubs. The office market is bifurcating: premium, spec-built GCC space will command 8-10% rental growth; bulk IT services space will see 2-3% rental decline. This is a 18-24 month structural shift that equity analysts have not yet priced in.","pct_10y":6,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 6th percentile is a 10-year low, but this metric is becoming obsolete as a proxy for IT sector health. The GCC shift is a structural reallocation of office demand away from traditional IT services — a trend that will accelerate as Indian IT services face margin pressure and GCCs expand.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

Services Carry Growth While Manufacturing Loses Altitude

The facts:

  • PMI Composite at 54.6 (83rd percentile) is services-driven at 54.5 — manufacturing PMI fell to 52.8 from 53.5, its third consecutive monthly decline.
  • IIP overall at 6.7% YoY — down from 8.8% — while core sector slipped to 5.4% YoY from 6.0%; upstream inputs are not keeping pace with capital goods orders.
  • Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile, up from 75.6%) is the one number that justifies the capex narrative — above the threshold where private investment historically follows.
  • But two-wheeler sales at 19.7% YoY and PV sales at 16% YoY signal rural and mass-market demand is holding, even as airline passengers at 86.4 mn / month sit at only the 35th percentile.

The tension: The headline GDP at 7.8% YoY is services-led and urban-skewed; manufacturing is losing momentum precisely as the capex cycle needs industrial output to validate it. A services economy cannot sustain 77% capacity utilisation in goods sectors.

Bottom line: Watch manufacturing PMI — a print below 52 would signal the capex cycle is running on financing momentum, not real demand.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

US Resilience, China Weakness — India Caught Between Both

The facts:

  • US PMI Composite at 56 (84th percentile) and US GDP SAAR rising to 2.2% SAAR from 1.5% — US growth is re-accelerating, which keeps the Fed on hold and the dollar bid.
  • But China GDP at 4.3% YoY (down from 5.0%) with PMI at 49.5 (contraction) removes the commodity reflation tailwind India's exporters were counting on.
  • US 10Y Treasury at 5.24% yield (95th percentile) — bond markets are tightening for the Fed; every 25 bps of yield rise pulls $1-2 bn of EM portfolio flows toward US fixed income.
  • BOJ at 1.0% p.a. (86th percentile, up from 0.75%) is the underappreciated tail: yen carry unwind is not priced into India's FII flow assumptions.

The tension: US resilience keeps global rates high and the dollar strong; China weakness removes the export and commodity demand buffer. India faces the worst combination — imported inflation from oil and imported tightening from US yields — with no offsetting global growth dividend.

Bottom line: If US 10Y holds above 5.25% yield through October, expect FII equity flows to turn negative within 4-6 weeks — watch the weekly FII data.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

Domestic Flows at Record Highs — But the Funding Gap Widens

The facts:

  • DII equity net flows at ₹58,502 cr net / month (100th percentile, rising two consecutive months) — the highest in the 10-year dataset; SIP inflows at ₹32,297 cr / month (92nd percentile).
  • SIP AUM at ₹18.62 lakh cr (93rd percentile) is growing faster than account count at 100.18 mn (82nd percentile) — average ticket size rising to ₹18,600 per account signals HNI/UHNI entry, not mass-market deepening.
  • But bank CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits (75th percentile) with credit at 17.1% YoY vs deposits at 10.8% YoY means the banking system is funding growth through costlier wholesale channels.
  • FII equity net at ₹29,631 cr net / month (83rd percentile) looks strong — but two months ago it was negative ₹3,112 cr net / month; the reversal is fragile and BOJ-sensitive.

The tension: Mutual fund flows are at record levels, but they are concentrated in affluent retail — not the broad-based SIP deepening that would make domestic liquidity structurally resilient. Meanwhile, the banking system's funding stress is worsening regardless of equity market inflows.

Bottom line: SIP YoY growth at 14% YoY (down from 16%) is the early warning — if it falls below 12% YoY, the HNI-driven SIP surge is masking underlying retail fatigue.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

Nifty in Five-Session Slide; REITs Repricing GCC Reality

The facts:

  • NRI buying is RISING — NRI share of residential purchases at 20% (up from 15%, +5 pp), with NRI share within premium/luxury at 25%; remittances at $73 bn (12.8% YoY) provide the funding.
  • Premium (₹80 lakh – ₹1.5 cr) and luxury (₹1.5 – 2.5 cr) together account for 58% of new supply launches — Hyderabad leads sales momentum at 15% YoY with launches up 120% YoY; NCR sales at -1% YoY.
  • Nifty 50 at 22,422 has fallen five consecutive sessions from 23,447 — India VIX at 14.46 (up four of last five observations) signals the complacency is unwinding.
  • But Embassy REIT at ₹370/unit, Mindspace at ₹345/unit, Brookfield at ₹263/unit — all down 13-31% from prior prints — are pricing the office absorption collapse at the 6th percentile before the GCC re-rating has been understood.

The tension: REIT prices are being marked down on aggregate office absorption data, but GCCs now represent 42% of occupier demand and are leasing premium space at rising rents — the index-level absorption number is the wrong signal for REIT NAV.

Bottom line: Embassy and Mindspace REITs are a buy if GCC leasing in Bengaluru (vacancy 11.4%, rents at ₹102/sqft/mo) holds — watch Q4 GCC deal announcements as the trigger.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Three Fuses, One Match — Oil, Rates, and the Deposit Gap

The facts:

  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) with Brent at $102.25/bbl — every $10/bbl adds ~$15 bn to India's annual import bill, widens CAD by ~40 bps, and pushes INR toward 97-98.
  • US 10Y at 5.24% yield (95th percentile) — sustained above 5.25% yield triggers EM carry unwind; FII flows flipped negative as recently as two months ago at -₹3,112 cr net / month.
  • CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits with NBFC credit accelerating to 14.9% YoY — wholesale-funded NBFCs face margin compression; a liquidity event in one mid-sized NBFC could reprice the entire sector.
  • But India VIX at 14.46 (10th percentile) remains historically low — options are cheap, which means the market is not yet hedging the tail.

The tension: All three risks — oil, global rates, and domestic funding stress — are individually manageable; the danger is their interaction. Oil widens CAD, which weakens INR, which accelerates FII outflows, which tightens domestic liquidity, which stresses NBFC funding. The chain is short.

Bottom line: Watch Brent crude this week — a close above $105/bbl triggers the full CAD-INR-FII feedback loop and forces RBI's hand on FX intervention.

"}
